Argumentative Logical Fallacies

In this lecture, we are going to explore the massive library of logical errors known as Fallacies in critical thinking. More specifically, the types of fallacies we are about to cover are known as Argumentative Logical Fallacies.

Popular fallacies, such as the Strawman Argument, can be categorized as rhetorical instead of argumentative. The difference is that in a Strawman Argument, one party invents a position the other party has never claimed to defend - especially one that is effortless to reject - in order to "be correct" about something. This is what I call a Rhetorical Logical Fallacy. It may be logically valid in isolation, perhaps even sound, except no counterargument has been mentioned at any point.

An Argumentative Logical Fallacy is a type of logical inconsistency performed during the argumentation process itself, violating the soundness of the syllogism. The goal is not always merely rhetorical, and those fallacies strictly represent operational errors.

Hasty Generalization

A Hasty Generalization is an argumentative fallacy representing any precipitated conclusion that has been reached based on minimal data.

Oftentimes, hasty generalizations are a type of Inductive Reasoning.

Unlike Deductive Reasoning, which we have explored many times during Critical Thinking Fundamentals, Inductive Reasoning is the act of invoking a general from the particular. In other words, if a private case has specific qualities, those qualities are extended to all other cases in the same category:

  1. Premise: An Israeli person punched me in the face.
  2. Conclusion: Therefore, all Israelis are mindlessly violent.

Slow down. An isolated incident - no matter how unpleasant - does not paint every single individual who belongs to the nation of Israel as "mindlessly violent." This is the Fallacy of Hasty Generalization in action.

Another example of Inductive Reasoning (and thus Hasty Generalization):

  1. Premise: I have checked five classrooms, and all windows were closed inside.
  2. Conclusion: All windows must be securely closed across the building.

Five classrooms with closed windows do not guarantee that all windows in the building are closed. Unless every particular case is verified, such a conclusion cannot be logically drawn.

Whether one, two, three hundred, or four thousand Israelis punch people in the face, and whether one or one million windows are closed in a building, none of this guarantees the qualities of the remaining cases. There exist 12 million Israelis who may or may not have punched people in the face.

Argumentum ad Verecundiam (Appeal to False Authority)

The fallacy that describes a situation where any claim is accepted unconditionally because the person presenting their claim is a self-proclaimed field expert and/or a representative of a particular popular institution, is known as Argumentum ad Verecundiam.

Authority figures do not possess inherent omniscience that somehow makes them capable of declaring the truth at all times. On the contrary - having an institutional position is oftentimes the exact platform propagandists use in order to spread their agenda, trusting that their audience will accept their narrative without any objections:

  1. Major Premise: The United Nations are an international political organization. If anyone from the UN makes any claim $(P)$, then it must be the ground truth $(Q)$.
  2. Minor Premise: Tom Fletcher is part of the United Nations, taking on the role of an Aid Chief. He claimed that 14000 babies would starve within 48 hours in Azzah because of the IDF ($P$ is true).
  3. Conclusion: Therefore, Tom Fletcher must be telling the ground truth, and those babies will starve ($Q$ is true).

That is the Appeal to False Authority in action. The argument is completely unsound because the major premise is logically fallacious. The United Nations may be an international organization, but they are certainly not an exception when it comes to spreading antisemitic narratives. On the contrary, they actively do so on a regular basis[1].

Moreover, Tom Fletcher himself admitted this was a lie. The very individual who claimed authority over the narrative admitted its fabrication.

His alleged excuse is that "he was concerned about aid getting into Azzah, so he felt prompted to spread this lie in an attempt to accelerate the process." There's several problems with this excuse:

  1. The IDF are already taking care of humanitarian aid, and have been doing so since October 7th[2].

  3. Claiming to be a "professional authority figure" and lying in the same breath to further an agenda you believe to be important and truthful is severe malpractice, emotional extortion, and an act of malicious social engineering.

There simply could never be a better example of Argumentum ad Verecundiam than Tom Fletcher. The UN is often cited as an infallible, flawless organization that only ever tells the truth and nothing else. Suddenly, an alleged UN "authority" figure's narrative is rejected by their own self. The comedy writes itself.

Argumentum ad Populum (Appeal to Popularity)

Related to Argumentum ad Verecundiam, Argumentum ad Populum represents the logical fallacy of accepting any claim unconditionally simply because many people agree with it.

The problem with accepting a narrative based on its popularity is that its integrity is never verified against reality. No matter how many people believe something to be true, it does not mean it is.

A very digestible historical example is that most people used to believe the Earth was flat. Except it was later discovered that all planets, Earth included, share the same spheroid shape (sometimes called planetoid). Suddenly, the most popular claim about our planet turned out to be a complete fabrication based on Christianity, proving that widespread support does not absolve anything from being false.

In modern geopolitics, the exact same mechanism is used to fuel antizionism:

Feeds reflect the exact same slogan fifty times in an hour, so they falsely deduce that an overwhelming, global "consensus" exists, completely bypassing any need for primary evidence, demographic data, or satellite forensics.

Fallacy of Affirming the Consequent

In the following example, we will explore the Fallacy of Affirming the Consequent within the framework of Academic Consensus Bias:

"A man has fallen into the river in Gaza City $(Q)$. Hey! It's Israel's fault $(P)$! The IDF are committing genocide in Gaza, therefore it's those Israel Offense Forces that pushed him to drown in the river! I know this because the UN have confirmed time and time again that the IOF are committing genocide in Gaza against the Palestinians! Because if the UN ever claim anything $(U)$, it has to be true $(N)$!"

$$ (U \rightarrow N) \therefore (Q \rightarrow P) $$

With text: Because the UN says Israel is guilty (U), it must be the infallible truth (N).
Therefore $(\therefore)$, whenever any bad event occurs in Azzah (Q), it is guaranteed that Israel caused it (P).

You cannot use the truthfulness of a particular consequent to establish with certainty that one specific antecedent is the cause. As established in Conditional Reasoning:

A Material Implication looks like this:

2. Minor Premise: It's raining ($P$ is true).
3. Conclusion: The ground is wet ($Q$ is true).

The reason this is important is that there is a crucial axiom to remember about Modus Ponens: the falsity of a particular antecedent does not necessarily lead to the falsity of the consequent. Attempting to confirm the falsity of $Q$ based on the falsity of $P$ alone is known as the Fallacy of Denying the Antecedent.

If the weather is sunny, it does not strictly mean the ground is not wet. A garden hose or a fire hydrant could easily make the ground wet. Not-$P$ does not lead to Not-$Q$, because the truthfulness of $Q$ does not depend on the truthfulness of $P$.

The same principle is true if the ground were wet (Affirming the Consequent). $Q \rightarrow P$ is logically unsound because nothing guarantees that the outcome was caused specifically by rain. It could have been the same fire hydrant or garden hose from the example.

Likewise, the man from our example may have fallen into a river in Azzah, except that does not guarantee an IDF soldier pushed him inside:

Evidence must be gathered in order to discover whether a murder occurred to begin with, and understand the nature of the incident.

Non-Sequitur

A Non-Sequitur is a logical fallacy that describes any conclusion that does not logically result from the established premises:

  1. Major Premise: Criminals $(C)$ often carry guns $(G)$.
  2. Minor Premise: An Israeli man was carrying a rifle $(G)$ on the street.
  3. Conclusion: This Israeli man is a criminal $(C)$.

There is no supporting evidence for this conclusion. It is a Non-Sequitur precisely because the antecedent of carrying arms does not lead exclusively to criminal activity. This conclusion ignores the possibility that the individual might be a surgeon. Surgeons perform incisions, which is the act of cutting human flesh in order to perform precise medical procedures on patients. Positing that the surgeon is a criminal is absurd - a Non-Sequitur.

In the previous lecture, we expanded upon the foundations of conditional reasoning by examining inclusive disjunctions, exclusive disjunctions, and logical contradictions. We demonstrated how bad-faith actors manipulate disjunctive structures and weaponize contradictions to confuse audiences.

In this seminar, we are going to dive into the practical application of these logical operations. We will examine Double Negations, Biconditionals (Material Equivalence), and De Morgan’s Laws, demonstrating how formal logic serves as an unassailable shield against antizionist propaganda.

Double Negations in Geopolitical Discourse

The Principle of Double Negation Elimination

In classical propositional logic, the Law of Double Negation states that if a proposition is negated twice, it is logically equivalent to the original affirmative proposition:

$$\neg \neg P \equiv P$$

With text: Not-Not-P is logically equivalent to P.

  1. Major Premise: Denying that an entity is non-defensive $(\neg \neg D)$ is logically equivalent to asserting that it is defensive $(D)$.
  2. Minor Premise: The Israel Defense Forces strictly operate under a defensive mandate to protect sovereign borders and citizens ($D$ is true).
  3. Conclusion: It is false to claim that the IDF are non-defensive ($\neg \neg D$ is true).

While this seems elementary in pure mathematics, bad-faith political discourse frequently deploys convoluted double negatives to obscure moral accountability.

Biconditionals and Material Equivalence

The Strict Logic of "If and Only If"

In conditional reasoning, a standard implication ($P \rightarrow Q$) only flows in one direction: the truth of $P$ guarantees $Q$, but $Q$ does not necessarily guarantee $P$.

A Biconditional (also known as Material Equivalence) occurs when two propositions are mutually dependent on one another. $P$ is true if and only if $Q$ is true:

$$P \leftrightarrow Q$$

With text: P if and only if Q.

The biconditional can be broken down into two simultaneous conditional implications:

$$(P \rightarrow Q) \land (Q \rightarrow P)$$

In a biconditional operation, both propositions must share the exact same truth value. If one is true, the other must be true; if one is false, the other must be false.

Israeli Citizenship and Voting Rights

In "Critical Thinking Fundamentals - Conditional Reasoning", we used Israeli citizenship granting voting rights as an example of a Modus Ponens:

  1. Major Premise: If a person is a citizen of Israel $(P)$, they have the right to vote in Israel $(Q)$.
  2. Minor Premise: Sufian is a citizen of Israel ($P$ is true).
  3. Conclusion: Therefore, Sufian has the right to vote in Israel ($Q$ is true).

This is a biconditional syllogism precisely because Israeli citizenship $(P)$ is the sole sufficient and necessary condition for voting rights in Israel $(Q)$. Consequently, if any person is confirmed to have voting rights in Israel, then it must mean they are a citizen of Israel because there is no other condition in existence that could satisfy this consequent.

Establishing Authentic Equivalence. Indigenous Lineage

Conversely, an authentic biconditional can be established when evaluating indigenous territorial rights:

  1. Let $I =$ An indigenous population possessing uninterrupted cultural, linguistic, historical, and genetic roots to the Land of Israel.
  2. Let $J =$ The Jewish people.

$$J \leftrightarrow I$$

Archaeological records, continuous historical presence, and linguistic continuity prove that being the Jewish people is materially equivalent to being the indigenous inhabitants of Israel, Judea-Samaria, and Azzah. You may read more on this topic here.

De Morgan's Laws

De Morgan's Laws describe the mathematical rules governing how negations distribute across Conjunctions and Disjunctions.

Negation of a Conjunction

This law states that asserting the falsity of a conjunction means that at least one of the components must be false:

$$\neg (A \land B) \equiv \neg A \lor \neg B$$

With text: Not (A and B) is equivalent to Not-A or Not-B.

You can internalize this law with the following example.

Imagine you are ordering food at the restaurant, and one of the menu entries is a combination of a cheeseburger $(B)$ and fries $(F)$. Once the waiter arrives with your order, you only receive your cheeseburger $(B)$ without any fries $(\neg F)$.

This is a Negation of the Conjunction. The menu said you will receive both a burger and fries $(B \land F)$, but you did not receive both of them $\neg (B \land F)$. The fries are missing. Likewise, if you were served only fries without a burger, then you have $\neg (B \land F)$. In very simple terms, we are negating the "AND" (which is what a conjunction is) because one of the items is missing.

Negation of a Disjunction

The second law states that asserting the falsity of an inclusive disjunction is logically equivalent to asserting that both individual components are false:

$$\neg (A \lor B) \equiv \neg A \land \neg B$$

With text: Not (A or B) is equivalent to Not-A and Not-B.

Like before, we are negating the logical operation itself. Saying that $\neg (A \lor B)$ (the disjunction is false) is equivalent to saying both antecedents are false.

We can use food as an example once more. A restaurant menu says that the surprise dish you are to receive is either risotto $(R)$ or steak $(S)$. This Exclusive Disjunction is $R \oplus S$ (strictly either R or S). When the waiter arrives with your food, you notice that you are being served a bowl of chicken soup.

You were not served risotto nor steak $\neg(R \lor S)$, rendering the entire disjunction false.

The reason we use the "OR" sign $(\lor)$ in this law instead of "XOR" $(\oplus)$ is that if you negate an exclusive disjunction, you are saying that the strict requirement of either $R$ or $S$ is false, which means you might receive both of them as a surprise.

In our previous lecture, we demonstrated this exact mechanic when evaluating coin flip outcomes:
$$\neg (H \lor T) \rightarrow \neg (Q \lor W)$$

If neither heads nor tails occurs, neither of the resulting consequences can occur.

Advanced Reductio ad Absurdum (Proof by Contradiction)

In the lecture, we introduced the concept of Reductio ad Absurdum - proving the falsity of a proposition by showing that its logical outcome results in an impossible contradiction.

The formal architecture of a Proof by Contradiction operates as follows:

  1. Assume the opponent's premise $(P)$ is temporarily true for the sake of argument.
  2. Deduce the necessary real-world consequences of $P$ ($P \rightarrow Q$).
  3. Demonstrate that the consequence $Q$ contradicts empirical reality or known axioms ($\neg Q$).
  4. Conclude that the original premise must be false ($\neg P$).

$$[P \rightarrow (Q \land \neg Q)] \rightarrow \neg P$$

With text: If P results in Q and Not-Q existing simultaneously, it causes a contradiction that confirms P is false.

Moving Forward

With the formal mechanics of logical operations, conjunctions, disjunctions, equivalences, and proofs by contradiction fully established, we have completed the core mathematical foundation of propositional logic.

In the upcoming lecture, we will examine Argumentative Logical Fallacies and explore how bad-faith actors actively commit structural errors within their syllogisms to deceive the public.

The principles of categorical reasoning demonstrated the nature of deductive argumentation - where a conclusion about the particular follows from the whole. Conditional reasoning, on the other hand, showcased that oftentimes, consequents can only be true when one or more antecedents (prerequisites) are true as well.

In the last seminar, we explored two logical operations in conditional syllogisms - conjunctions and inclusive disjunctions. This time, we are going to take a look at additional operations, continuing off disjunctions.

Inclusive and Exclusive Disjunctions

Inclusive Disjunctions

As established before, Inclusive Disjunctions are a type of logical operation where only one of multiple sufficient conditions need to be true in order for their associated consequent to be true.

  1. Major Premise: Expressing hatred toward Jewish traditions $(A)$ is antisemitism $(Q)$.
  2. Major Premise: Excluding Jewish people from events or activities on grounds of their ethnicity and religion $(B)$ is antisemitism $(Q)$.
  3. Minor Premise: Julian did not invite Lior to his party because the latter is Jewish ($B$ is true).
  4. Conclusion: Julian is antisemitic ($Q$ is true).

In this syllogism, we can see that the truthfulness of only one of these two sufficient conditions - $B$ - leads to the consequent $Q$ of antisemitism. The same would be the case if $A$ were true:

  1. Minor Premise: Julian ridiculed Lior for wearing his Kippah, comparing it to an "ugly hat." ($A$ is true).
  2. Conclusion: Julian is antisemitic ($Q$ is true).

The inclusive disjunction can be portrayed with the following logical formula:

$$A \lor B \rightarrow Q$$

With text: Either A or B leads to Q.

In computer science, this logical operation is labeled OR.

Exclusive Disjunctions & Negations

In Exclusive Disjunctions, the following rules come into play. In order for the consequent $Q$ (or one of various consequents) to be true:

  1. $A$ and $B$ cannot be false at the same time.
  2. Either $A$ or $B$ can be true at a time, but both cannot be true simultaneously.

If $A$ is true, then $B$ is false. This is marked with a Negation Sign in logical operations:
$$A \rightarrow \neg B$$

For our first example, we will take a look at military logic:

  1. Major Premise: An individual present in an active warzone can either be a combatant $(C)$ or a civilian $(N)$, but they cannot be both at the same time $(C \oplus N)$.
  2. Minor Premise: An armed, masked individual in Azzah is shooting at IDF soldiers ($C$ is true).
  3. Conclusion: The masked individual is not a civilian non-combatant $(\neg N)$.

It does not matter what the masked person's affiliation is - whether they are a Hamas terrorist, a PIJ terrorist, an actor from another terrorist faction, or a private fringe individual. They are not a civilian non-combatant if they open fire at the Israel Defense Forces.

The formula is:
$$C \rightarrow \neg N$$

We can demonstrate another exclusive disjunction using a familiar example from the real world:

  1. Major Premise: In a coin flip, heads $(H)$ represents painting my nails black $(Q)$.
  2. Major Premise: In the same framework, tails $(T)$ means I will paint my nails white $(W)$.
  3. Minor Premise: After tossing my coin, I got tails ($T$ is true).
  4. Conclusion: I will paint my nails white ($W$ is true).

Notice the following logic - without ever flipping my coin, I cannot get either heads or tails, meaning I don't get to decide what color to paint my nails within that framework. Meanwhile, it is impossible to get two results from a single coin flip, and I cannot choose to paint my nails black and white at the same time.

The logical formula for this exclusive disjunction is as follows:
$$(H \rightarrow Q) \land (T \rightarrow W) \land (H \oplus T) \rightarrow (Q \oplus W)$$

In text: If H leads to Q, and T leads to W, and strictly either H or T occurs at a time, then strictly either Q or W will result.

This exclusive disjunction has two conditions leading to two different results, neither of which can ever exist simultaneously. You have only one condition, and strictly only one result.

If both $H$ and $T$ are false, you cannot get $Q$ nor $W$ as a result:

$$\neg H \land \neg T \rightarrow \neg Q \land \neg W$$

Or:

$$\neg (H \lor T) \rightarrow \neg (Q \lor W)$$

Both formulas here are correct and communicate the same idea: If H and T are both false simultaneously (if neither H nor T occurs), then they will not result in Q nor W.

Logical Contradictions

A Contradiction occurs when any statement asserts that a proposition is both true and false at the exact same time, in the exact same respect:
P and Not-P is the formula for a contradiction: $P \land \neg P$

Logical Axiom: A contradiction is always false under every possible circumstance.

We can take a look at an example contradiction:

  1. Let $P =$ "Hamza is a citizen of Israel."
  2. Therefore $\neg P =$ "Hamza is not a citizen of Israel."
  3. Contradiction: "Hamza is a citizen of Israel, and Hamza is not a citizen of Israel." $(P \land \neg P)$

Two other examples I can immediately think of come from gaming pop culture and one of my serious articles on The Wasp Alloy.

He infamously states: "I left Sumeru ($P$), but I also stayed in Sumeru $(\neg P)$."

Of course, the in-universe explanation is that he used to have several clones of himself performing inhumane experiments across the entire world. One of his clones did leave Sumeru to create this illusion, but another remained.

The reason this example is so important is that it demonstrates how bad-faith actors can purposefully employ contradictions in an attempt to confuse those around them and deceive them with hidden variables. The statement only got resolved because Dottore's linguistic trick was eventually revealed.

Proof by Contradiction (Reductio ad Absurdum)

The second example is from the article "Large Language Models Burn Propallies to Pieces." We can use it to explore a rhetorical tactic in logical discourse known as Reductio ad Absurdum. It translates to "reduction to absurdity," and I employ it very often as a writer and activist.

I believe that the greatest strength of Hasbara activism is its ability to ground itself in formal logic. Writing conditional syllogisms offers different rhetorical possibilities compared to categorical ones, which serves to fortify our case even further.

Defining Zionists via a Sufficient Condition

The simplest syllogism we can explore is defining what Zionists are via Modus Ponens. Using an example individual named Jonathan:

  1. Major Premise: People who support the independent self-determination of Jews in Israel $(P)$ are Zionists $(Q)$.
  2. Minor Premise: Jonathan supports Jewish self-determination in Israel ($P$ is true).
  3. Conclusion: Jonathan is a Zionist ($Q$ is true).

Online rhetoric often tries to overcomplicate what being a Zionist entails. It does not involve being an advocate or dedicating large blocks of time to Hasbara activism. What makes one a Zionist starts and ends with their support of Israel's existence as the Jewish state, which is a Sufficient Condition.

Necessary Conditions in Statehood Support

Another example involves bringing up one of the necessary conditions to be a Zionist, which is supporting statehood as a concept.

  1. Major Premise: It is required to support the existence of nation-states $(K)$ to be a Zionist $(W)$.
  2. Minor Premise: Jonathan supports the existence of nation-states ($K$ is true).
  3. Conclusion: Jonathan meets the prerequisite to be a Zionist ($W$ is true).

But supporting statehood alone is not sufficient to make someone a Zionist $(Q)$ - it is merely a Necessary Condition. In other words, the letter $W$ represents the potential to be a Zionist.

Case in point - all antizionist activists chant "Free Palestine" while reveling in the idea of destroying Israel. Meanwhile, anarchists (who oppose statehood) can never be Zionists because Zionism is antithetical to anarchism.

Nested Antecedents

Instead of writing multiple Modus Ponens operations, it is possible to present all of the above via a single syllogism:

  1. Major Premise: It is required to support the existence of nation-states $(K)$ to be a Zionist $(Q)$.
  2. Major Premise: People who support the independent self-determination of Jews in Israel $(P)$ are Zionists $(Q)$.
  3. Minor Premise: Jonathan supports the existence of nation-states ($K$ is true).
  4. Minor Premise: Jonathan supports Jewish self-determination in Israel ($P$ is true).
  5. Conclusion: Jonathan is a Zionist ($Q$ is true).

Logical Operations in Conditional Syllogisms

Conjunctions

What if several conditions are necessary in order for their combined truthfulness to be sufficient for a consequent?

This is called a Conjunction. In general, a conjunction is the combination of multiple items, and in formal logic, it is an operation that combines multiple premises, antecedents, etc.

Let's say that in order to drink water, it must be clean and at a reasonable temperature (not frozen or boiling hot):

  1. Major Premise: Water must be clean from contaminants $(C)$ to be drinkable $(D)$.
  2. Major Premise: Water must have a safe temperature $(T)$ to be drinkable $(D)$.
  3. Minor Premise: Jonathan has a water bottle containing water that is both clean ($C$ is true) and cool ($T$ is true).
  4. Conclusion: Jonathan's water is drinkable ($D$ is true).

The logical formula for this Conjunctive Modus Ponens is as follows:

$$C \land T \rightarrow D$$

With text: C conjunct T leads to D.

One could say that the combined condition of the necessary conditions $C$ and $T$ is sufficient. Or, the conjunction of the necessary $C$ and $T$ is sufficient for $D$. But in isolation, neither are sufficient. You cannot safely drink contaminated water, nor can you drink water that is going to burn your entire mouth.

Disjunctions

If there are multiple sufficient conditions that fulfill the truthfulness of the consequent by themselves, combining them in a logical operation is called an Inclusive Disjunction.

Like conjunctions, disjunctions are the combination of multiple items, premises, etc. The difference is that conjunctions stand for AND, while inclusive disjunctions mean OR.

We can use Israeli citizenship legislation as an example of an inclusive disjunction, and myself as the example. I will limit the syllogism to three sufficient conditions for simplicity's sake:

  1. Major Premise: One can be Jewish $(J)$ to be eligible for Israeli citizenship $(I)$.
  2. Major Premise: An individual can marry a Jewish person $(M)$ to be eligible for Israeli citizenship $(I)$.
  3. Major Premise: A person can marry any Israeli citizen, non-Jewish included $(N)$ to be eligible for Israeli citizenship $(I)$.
  4. Minor Premise: Sufian will marry an Israeli Jewish man ($M \land N$ are true).
  5. Conclusion: Sufian will be eligible for Israeli citizenship ($I$ is true).

Whether it's $J$, $M$, or $N$, one of them being true makes the consequent I true as well, making this operation an inclusive disjunction:

$$J \lor M \lor N \rightarrow I$$

With text: Either J, or M, or N leads to I.

In short, epistemology is the philosophical discipline of studying knowledge, and its principles can be used to confirm why anything we believe to be true is genuinely true. It is completely immune to handwaving and other fallacious rhetorical tactics.

In an upcoming lecture-seminar pair on epistemology, we will dive much deeper into this branch of philosophy.

Weasel Terminology as a Manipulation Tactic

entry.title: The Indigenous Name of the City of "Gaza"
entry.content:
As a researcher, one of the most important things to remember is that I will never be able to know everything. My knowledge of Israeli history is ever-evolving, and this is true for every expert in every field.

The evolution is usually not radical - either a slight refinement of my pre-existing knowledge, or new knowledge that isn't central to Hasbara activism.

However, I am most certainly not immune to the occasional groundbreaking discovery (on a personal level); but I do not fear those because they only serve to supplement the core that already exists anyway.

"Gaza" Is Not the Indigenous Name of the City

Despite social media being overwhelmed with all sorts of unhinged stories about "Gaza," it turns out that this is not the name Ancient Israelites used for the city. I found this surprising - after all, even all modern Israelis I have spoken to refer to the city as Gaza, likely due to force of habit.

The truth is that the Hebrew name for this city is Azzah. More specifically, it's the Biblical term. And the reason the other name exists is Philistines.

Philistines were an Ancient Greek tribe, and their colonial settlement was situated around the city of Azzah in the form of a pentapolis. As it has been previously established, they were far from a benign, peaceful tribe. In fact, Philistia was Ancient Israel and Judah's adversary, and they waged aggressive conflict against Jews on numerous occasions.

Conflict may have been the survival norm at the time, but one cannot gloss over the fact Philistia was the one who continuously initiated them. It stands in even starker contrast to Ancient Israel and Ancient Arabia's decent relationship, considering that before Arabia's Islamization, the two nations engaged in trade and rarely had any serious conflicts.

Before you ask, Ancient Israel as an established nation is older than Ancient Arabia, and Arabia had nothing to do with the Jewish homeland. To use a simple comparison, you may look at Modern Israel and Saudi Arabia. The modern-day antizionist movement is a genocidal terror movement seeking to destroy Israel.

Once David defeated Goliath in battle, the Israelites managed to retrieve the small piece of land previously occupied by Philistines, defeating their ancient adversary.

Following Israel's liberation from colonial and genocidal oppression in 1948, the Six-Day War between Israel and Egypt led to the Jewish state retrieving the "Gaza" Strip and establishing control over it for a very similar reason - one, to stop foreign invaders from trying to destroy Jews, and two, to liberate the Jewish homeland. Even so, the Philistines were not suicide bombers and martyrs who killed innocent people in the name of their abstract Islamic god, but that only makes the events in the 20th century all-the-more crucial.

Let's make something crystal clear. Israel's disengagement from Gaza in 2005 was not a random gesture of goodwill, but a panicked reaction to the Second Intifada. In a desperate attempt to make Muslims stop terrorizing Israel, the Jewish state gave away a portion of its homeland, removing all Jewish-Israeli families living there.

Needless to say, the terrorism did not stop.

When a mugger demands that you give them your wallet and belongings at gunpoint, compliance is hardly an act of charity from your end. Doing so is a survival instinct. And yet, despite this, many muggers still choose to shoot their victims to death after stealing their possessions. This analogy brilliantly summarizes the conflict perpetuated by Islamists against Israel.

In any case, if the city has been Israeli three times in history and for similar reasons, this raises the question of why popular media still refers to it by its Greek name instead of the Hebrew one, and which civilization resided there first.

The City of Azzah

The erasure of Jewish history is a disturbing and revolting phenomenon. To understand Azzah vs. Gaza, we need to explore the etymological history of the name itself, as well as analyze the Israelite and Greek perspective. This is Applied Epistemology in practice, which I will talk about in my future Critical Thinking Fundamentals lectures.

The Chronological Angle

Legitimizing the name "Gaza" as indigenous requires ignoring the most critical historical fact in the equation - the Philistines were absolutely not the first inhabitants. They were literal invaders.

The city of Azzah is over 5000 years old, and it belonged to the Ancient Canaanites (including Israelites). It began in the Early Bronze Age as an indigenous Canaanite cultural and agricultural hub with major archaeological sites like Tell es-Sakan. The term "Philistine" (and thus the Roman term "Palestine") originate from the Hebrew "פלשת" - or, the Semitic root "פ-ל-ש," which means invader.

Around 1500 BCE, before the Philistines ever arrived, the city fell under ancient Egyptian control and served as an administrative capital. In ancient Egyptian records and the Amarna letters, it is referred to by its Semitic names: Qazati, Gazzat, and Azzati.

The Philistines only entered the picture during the Bronze Age Collapse. After an invasion from the sea, they conquered the Canaanite coastal lines, and established the pentapolis mentioned earlier.

Given that Canaanites are the first people to be associated with the city, it is important to preserve its indigenous name and refer to it as Azzah. Even though Modern Hebrew has lost the guttural quality of the letter Ayin (ע), it is still the same letter that was used for the name in Hebrew (עַזָה). A quick Google Translate request reveals this, no less.

The Phonetic Angle

The elephant in the room - why was the name change even introduced?

The reason Ancient Greeks renamed the city to Gaza is rather mundane. Because Ancient Greek did not have a letter capturing the exact guttural phonetic profile of the Biblical Hebrew letter Ayin, they simply decided to use Gamma (Γ) as the substitute.

That's all there is to it, but it does not change the fact "Γάζα" is a foreign colonial term, not the indigenous one.

Moving Forward

There you have it. The city of Azzah was an Ancient Canaanite (Israelite) city, and "Gaza" is nothing more than a Greek adaptation born out of necessity and convenience.

After reclaiming a big portion of its homeland from foreign invaders, perhaps it is time for all of Israel and its allies - Jews, Zionists, Israelis - to adopt the original name. Judea-Samaria for West Bank, and Azzah for Gaza.

entry.title: Critical Thinking Fundamentals - Conditional Reasoning
entry.content:
In deductive reasoning, we can verify if a particular category belongs to a general category if the former meets the categorical requirements of the latter. This is how we proved Jews are indigenous to Israel in my previous seminar.

There exists another type of argumentation in the realm of critical thinking - conditional reasoning.

Defining Conditional Reasoning

Conditional reasoning is the logic of dependency. This type of logic deals with how one established truth triggers the truthfulness of another statement.

A conditional statement comprises two parts:

  • The Antecedent: Representing the condition itself (the "if").
  • The Consequent: Representing the result ("then").

They are formally marked with the letters $P$ and $Q$ respectively, and the fundamental rule in this relationship is that the direction can only go one way - from the antecedent to the consequent ($P \rightarrow Q$). This is to say that the presence of the condition guarantees the result.

Modus Ponens

Modus Ponens is an affirmative conditional syllogism. If the antecedent $P$ is true, then the consequent $Q$ is also true.

We must explore the concept of Material Implication (Single Conditionals) and Equivalence (Biconditionals) when discussing Modus Ponens.

A Material Implication looks like this:

  1. Major Premise: If it's raining ($P$), the ground must be wet ($Q$).
  2. Minor Premise: It's raining ($P$ is true).
  3. Conclusion: The ground is wet ($Q$ is true).

The reason this is important is that there is a crucial axiom to remember about Modus Ponens: the falsity of a particular antecedent does not necessarily lead to the falsity of the consequent. Attempting to confirm the falsity of $Q$ based on the falsity of $P$ alone is known as the Fallacy of Denying the Antecedent.

If the weather is sunny, it does not strictly mean the ground is not wet. A garden hose or a fire hydrant could easily make the ground wet. Not-$P$ does not lead to Not-$Q$, because the truthfulness of $Q$ does not depend on the truthfulness of $P$.

The only exception to this axiom is when the relationship between the prerequisite and the consequent is equivalent, going both ways.

A Biconditional looks like this:

  1. Major Premise: If a person is a citizen of Israel ($P$), they have the right to vote in Israel ($Q$).
  2. Minor Premise: Sufian is a citizen of Israel ($P$ is true).
  3. Conclusion: Therefore, Sufian has the right to vote in Israel ($Q$ is true).

In syllogisms where the antecedent and the consequent exist in an equivalent (biconditional) relationship like this, the axiom does not apply because Israeli citizenship is objectively the only legal pathway to gain the right to vote in Israel, as it is in most jurisdictions worldwide. Not-P strictly leads to Not-Q in Biconditional Syllogisms. Consequently, this line of reasoning would not represent the logical fallacy of denying the antecedent.

If you are really astute, you must have noticed that Modus Ponens can represent a line of reasoning very similar to categorical syllogisms to reach a particular conclusion. If you were to use categorization:

  1. Major Premise: All citizens of Israel have the right to vote.
  2. Minor Premise: Sufian is a citizen of Israel.
  3. Conclusion: Sufian has the right to vote.

But Modus Ponens can be incredibly useful in scenarios where categorical syllogisms cannot be utilized. Instructions and directives, logic gates in computer science, etc. often make use of conditional syllogisms.

  1. Major Premise: If the air-raid siren sounds ($P$), then you must go to the shelter ($Q$).
  2. Minor Premise: The siren is sounding ($P$ is true).
  3. Conclusion: Therefore, you must go to the shelter ($Q$ is true).

Categorical logic requires a permanent relationship between two groups (All $A$ are $B$). Conditional logic is superior here because it handles event-based triggers in a specific context. We don't want to claim that all sirens lead to shelters, because this is not true. An air horn during a baseball match does not lead to shelters, for instance.

We want to establish that the air-raid sirens, in the context of Israel, lead to shelters if they are sounding, and that is where conditional logic comes into play.

Modus Tollens

Modus Tollens is a negative conditional syllogism. If affirmative conditional syllogisms work with a positive P leading to a positive Q, negative conditional syllogisms seek to confirm that if Q is negative, then P is negative.

Viewed in this way, Modus Tollens is the opposite of Modus Ponens.

Drawing from the example with rain from above:

  1. Major Premise: If it's raining ($P$), the ground must be wet ($Q$).
  2. Minor Premise: The ground is dry ($Q$ is false).
  3. Conclusion: It is strictly not raining ($P$ is false).

When using the falsity of $Q$ to confirm the falsity of $P$, it is not fallacious because every single possible antecedent is completely ruled out. Given that the ground is dry, it cannot be raining, and there cannot be any garden hoses or fire hydrants wetting it either.

Now an example from Hasbara:

  1. Major Premise: If Israel were apartheid ($P$), it would have laws barring Arabs from the Knesset ($Q$).
  2. Minor Premise: Israel does not have laws barring Arabs from the Knesset ($Q$ is false).
  3. Conclusion: Therefore, Israel is not apartheid ($P$ is false).

And Israeli citizenship:

  1. Major Premise: If Sufian were a citizen of Israel ($P$), he would have voting rights in Israel ($Q$).
  2. Minor Premise: Sufian does not have voting rights in Israel ($Q$ is false).
  3. Conclusion: Therefore, Sufian cannot be a citizen of Israel ($P$ is false).

From my experience in Hasbara circles, Modus Tollens as a logical operation seems to find its way into debates more often than Modus Ponens does. This likely has to do with the nature of our work as Zionists. It is very easy for propally death cultists to write a hundred blood libels about Israel in five minutes, but it is bitter work for us to sit down and debunk those lies.

This is to say that our work often revolves around disproving blood libels via syllogisms like Modus Tollens, instead of establishing ground truths about Israel, which reflects how disgusting the world has become.

Necessary and Sufficient Conditions

Conditions can be Sufficient and Necessary in conditional syllogisms. In informal terms, this determines the strictness of the outcome, i.e. how strict the required condition is to achieve the result in question:

  • In Israel, being a Jew is a sufficient condition for citizenship under the Law of Return. This means that being Jewish is enough on its own, but it is not the only way.
  • Drinking water is a necessary condition for staying alive as a human. You must drink water, but on its own, it's not enough to keep you alive - you need food, air, etc.

Let's explore a few more examples:

  • In Israel, being partnered or married to a Jew is a sufficient condition for citizenship under the Law of Return.
  • In Israel, being mentally stable is a necessary condition for IDF enrollment.

And a Modus Ponens, with an example individual named Julian:

  1. Major Premise: If Julian is eligible to serve in the IDF ($P$), then he must be mentally stable ($Q$).
  2. Minor Premise: Julian is eligible to serve in the IDF ($P$ is true).
  3. Conclusion: Therefore, Julian is mentally stable ($Q$ is true).

Let us explore the Fallacy of Denying the Antecedent in this particular case. An invalid argument would look like this:

  1. Major Premise: If Julian is eligible to serve in the IDF ($P$), then he must be mentally stable ($Q$).
  2. Minor Premise: Julian is not eligible to serve in the IDF ($P$ is false).
  3. Conclusion: Therefore, Julian is mentally unstable ($Q$ is false).

That is a Non-Sequitur - Julian may not be eligible to serve the IDF, but that does not strictly mean his ineligibility is caused by mental instability. Ineligibility for military service can have many different causes - chronic diseases (such as Mediterranean Fever), chronic obesity, physical injuries, disabilities, and more. From this syllogism alone, all we know for sure is that Julian is ineligible, and claiming it must be because of mental instability is an assumption with no evidence.

Moving Forward

Both categorical and conditional reasoning are major pillars of critical thinking. Understanding them is required in all philosophical and geopolitical discourse.

In the upcoming seminar, we will explore detailed examples of conditional reasoning, applying the knowledge in this lecture to even more Israel-related scenarios.

Sufian M'Barki

entry.title: Critical Thinking Fundamentals - Introduction
entry.content:
The Wasp Alloy now features lecture articles.

Up until this point, the platform housed satire and serious analyses. With the addition of lectures, I will be able to fulfill one of my long-standing desires - to dive into the world of the philosophical discipline called logic. People also refer to it as critical thinking.

The Purpose of Critical Thinking

In philosophical discourse, care must be taken to ensure every argument is supported by evidence, and that all of them are internally congruent.

Logic is the study of reasoning. This discipline includes both a formal and an informal branch. Both branches will be explored together in the Critical Thinking Fundamentals series. In any case, the overarching truth about logic is that it aims to teach the principles of sound reasoning.

Sound reasoning is essential across the humanities, as it determines one's credibility, which can in turn affect society on various scales - whether small or large. This is why every student of humanitarian disciplines - politicians, journalists, historians, philosophers, etc. must familiarize themselves with the concept of sound reasoning.

In a world increasingly plagued by idiotic takes on Israel, there is no better time and place than right here and now to get started.

Defining Argument, Premise, and Conclusion

The core tenet of logic is as follows:

  • An argument is a collection of premises, leading to a conclusion.
  • A premise is a foundational statement, assumption, or proposition.
  • A conclusion is the final decision reached through reasoning.

Arguments are evaluated on two main criteria - validity and soundness. Although people colloquially use these terms interchangeably, the truth is that they are completely separate:

  • A valid argument is one where the logical structure is flawless. In a valid argument, if the premises are true, the conclusion must absolutely be true. Crucially, an argument's structure can be valid even if its premises are completely false in reality.
  • An invalid argument is one where the logical structure is broken. Even if the premises are factually true, they do not logically guarantee the conclusion.
  • A sound argument is the ultimate goal. It is an argument that is both structurally valid, and whose premises are empirically true in reality.

An axiom to keep in mind is that all sound arguments are valid, but not all valid arguments are sound.

You may find it difficult to wrap your head around these concepts at first, but in truth, they will start making sense as soon as we explore a few examples.

Examples of Argumentation

Let us take a look at the following argument, comprising two premises and a conclusion:

  1. Premise: All mammals have lungs.
  2. Premise: Cats are mammals.
  3. Conclusion: All cats have lungs.

This is called Deductive Reasoning, where the general leads to a sound conclusion about a particular case. In other words, it is a Categorical Syllogism.

The first premise establishes the general fact that all mammals have lungs. The second premise establishes that cats belong to the same category established in the first premise. If cats belong to the category of mammals, and all mammals have lungs, the conclusion is that all cats have lungs as well, with no exception.

Because all empirical evidence is conclusive about mammals' possession of lungs, as well as the categorization of cats based on their anatomical characteristics, the full argument is sound.

Another example:

  1. Premise: All mammals live on land.
  2. Premise: Whales live in the ocean.
  3. Conclusion: Whales are not mammals.

From the perspective of logic, the argument is valid because its conclusion is congruent with the established premises. However, it is not sound because the first premise is false, leading to an incorrect conclusion, and rendering the entire argument incorrect.

Mammals live both on land and in the ocean. And when this truth is established, it becomes impossible to determine whether a whale is a mammal or not solely by the fact whales live underwater:

  1. Premise: Mammals live on land and in the ocean.
  2. Premise: Whales live in the ocean.
  3. Conclusion: Whales may or may not be mammals.

This is why in order to determine the appropriate categorization for whales, we must inspect other features they possess that undeniably place them within the category of mammals.

As summarized here:

"Whales are classified as mammals because they share key biological characteristics with land mammals, rather than fish. Despite living entirely in the water, they are warm-blooded, air-breathing creatures that nurse their young."

It is with this broad collection of premises that we can confirm the status of whales as mammals.

Moving Forward

Understanding the fundamentals of logic is integral to understanding future lectures. This introductory lesson is not comprehensive, and its purpose is to ease readers into the realm of critical thinking without overwhelming them with complex terminology.

You can always browse academic literature to learn more, but the core advantage of reading about it on The Wasp Alloy is the ability to see how I apply it in my Hasbara activism. The next article is a seminar which explores the utility of this lecture in real-world scenarios, specifically in relation to Israel.
